title: The Day the Depot Danced
markdown:
The tram depot usually hummed with engines, the clank of metal, and the honest scent of oil. Most folk knew it only from the pavement. It kept the town’s wheels turning. Today it threw its doors open for a grand unveiling, a splashy celebration of progress, and at the heart of the coordinating — with a dedication that would have pleased a field marshal — stood Iris the deer, botanical illustrator of meticulous line, and her older sister Yara, a mole as grounded as the earth she preferred.

Iris believed in precision. Her world was fine lines and scientific names, every petal accounted for. The depot plan was a symphony of speeches and posies, blueprints annotated, the flow of people imagined as smooth as polished brass. She adjusted a tiny bluebell in its pot until the bell pointed precisely north-east. “Everything must be just so.” Then, softer, as if reciting a charm: “The plan is still excellent. Reality is simply being overfamiliar.”

Yara wrinkled her nose. “Looks like fun. A bit tidy for my taste. A bit too much stillness.” She was a mole of tunnels and textures, damp soil and unexpected roots, more at home under the town than in its polished squares.

The gates swung. Families came in with balloons that bobbed like curious jellyfish. Grown-ups wore anticipation the way they wore their better coats. The air buzzed in a key the depot did not usually sing.

Then a gust — unpredicted, though Iris had consulted three almanacs — shouldered through the yard. It lifted the Welcome banner she had centred with a ruler’s conscience, spun it like a ribbon, and dropped it askew over the old repair bay, so that the maintenance wing received a dramatic and accidental greeting.

Iris’s hooves skittered on concrete. “The banner! It’s welcoming the wrong section!” The diagram in her head felt suddenly thin. Then, dry as a good pencil: perhaps the maintenance wing would enjoy the festive spirit.

Yara patted her shoulder with a strong paw. “A touch of the unexpected. Like a bold root through pavement. That’s exploration.”

Next, a young sprout no taller than a well-grown dandelion tripped over a velvet rope that had been, in hindsight, a little too proud of itself. He did not fall. His packet of rainbow sprinkles, intended for post-ceremony cupcakes, went airborne and showered Iris’s labelled ferns with confectionery confetti.

Iris winced. The labels, meant for the dignity of science, wore sugar. “Sparkly,” she managed.

“A flourish of natural colour!” Yara’s eyes shone like wet pebbles. “Interactive. The specimens are feeling quite spritely. You’re thinking outside the pot.”

The cascade continued, a run of small charming disarray. A forgotten leaky pipe, perhaps protesting its long silence, offered a gentle drip-drip-drip beside the vintage tram seating — watery percussion, a soundtrack no programme had printed. A squirrel bolder than any Iris had ever inked, tail flicking like a question mark, made a daring dash across the roof and dislodged a few loose tiles that clattered with a surprisingly musical opinion. With each mishap the crowd murmured, not in dismay, but in admiration. “Oh, look! She’s planned for that, too. Such foresight.” They saw not chaos but deliberate artistry, and Iris, who had never intended to be a conductor of accidents, felt the afternoon rewrite her reputation without asking.

Iris felt a warmth that was not the midday sun and was not the neat satisfaction of lines aligned. Yara had taken to demonstrating, to delighted toddlers now sporting very muddy knees, the best way to dig for worms. Faces were happy. They were not bothered by the misplaced banner or the sprinkle-dusted ferns. They were charmed. They were engaged. They were finding the afternoon in the untamed spirit of the moment, and Iris, watching, found a dawning amusement where her meteorology notes had failed.

Late light lengthened. The depot’s hard edges softened. Somewhere a tram bell, unused for the ceremony, gave a single unused note as if it too had opinions about openings. Iris remembered other yards: the first depot she had sketched as a fawn, all shadow and no people; a winter morning when Yara had brought her a root that looked like a question. Those memories arrived without asking, layered over the present clatter, and then receded. A stripe of sun cut a dusty pane and found a forgotten patch of chalk on the concrete, the ghost of a diagram Iris had drawn for optimal signage. It shimmered like butterfly dust, or like a star that had taken a wrong turning and did not mind.

The plan is still excellent. Reality is simply being overfamiliar.

Iris set her sketchbook down. That was all: a hoof opening, paper meeting floor, the diagram surrendering its claim to be the afternoon’s map. Yara ambled over and nudged her. “Remarkable. All those little surprises. The depot is singing.”

Iris looked at her sister, at the chatter, at laughter caught in the iron beams. She had not tamed a gathering. She had left a canvas, and the day had painted it with wind and sugar and drip and tile. “You know, Yara,” she said, and the precise cadence had gone out of her, “the plan is still excellent. Reality is simply being overfamiliar.” Rainbow dust caught on her nose. The bluebell still pointed north-east, loyal as a compass that had not been informed of the party. She did not pick the sketchbook up. The chalk-shine on the floor kept its own counsel, and the depot, for once, danced.
characters: Iris (a deer botanical illustrator), Yara (a mole older sister)
